titre: Diagnostic Performance of Radiomics-Based Machine Learning in Differentiating Glioblastoma From Brain Metastasis: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Hong C, Liu G, Bie Z, Guo Y, Du Y, Hu Y, Li S, Liu P.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review journal article
resume: Background Glioblastoma (GBM) and brain metastasis (BM) are the most common malignant intracranial tumors in adults. Noninvasive differentiation between them remains challenging, as they frequently share similar imaging features. Although radiomics-based machine learning (ML) models show promise, systematic evidence of their performance remains limited. Objective We aimed to systematically estimate the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models in differentiating GBM from BM and to explore multiclass classification involving primary central nervous system lymphoma (PCNSL), thereby assessing their potential for clinical use. Methods We systematically searched PubMed, Embase, Web of Science, and Cochrane Library databases from inception to January 22, 2026, for studies reporting the diagnostic performance of radiomics-based ML models for differentiating GBM from BM. Multiclass studies involving PCNSL were also retained. Methodological quality was appraised via the Radiomics Quality Score 2.0. Binary diagnostic accuracy was pooled using a bivariate random-effects model, stratified by internal and independent external validation. Multiclass sensitivities and specificities were pooled using separate joint generalized linear mixed models. Physician assessments were evaluated as an exploratory benchmark. Results A total of 39 studies (31 binary and 8 multiclass), involving 11,558 patients, were included. For binary classification, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 88.9% (95% CI 84.1%-92.4%) and 83.0% (95% CI 76.8%-87.9%) in internal validation, and 83.8% (95% CI 77.4%-88.7%) and 80.7% (95% CI 71.1%-87.7%) in external validation, respectively. In multiclass analyses, pooled sensitivity was 84.4% (95% CI 72.4%-91.8%) for GBM, 70.6% (95% CI 54.4%-82.8%) for BM, and 75.0% (95% CI 62.7%-84.3%) for PCNSL, with corresponding specificities of 82.5% (95% CI 70.1%-90.4%), 88.8% (95% CI 81.9%-93.3%), and 94.4% (95% CI 88.4%-97.4%), respectively. Conclusions Radiomics-based ML models could distinguish between GBM and BM in the included cohorts. However, due to methodological limitations and scarce evidence, their generalizability and clinical utility remain unclear. Further multicenter prospective studies should conduct independent external validation in consecutive patients. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420261295269; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261295269.

titre: External validation of an artificial intelligence-based ECG algorithm for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction: a prospective diagnostic cohort study.
auteurs: Champetier A, Lee MS, Lopez-Ayala P, Jo YY, Boeddinghaus J, Koechlin L, Bima P, Crisanti L, Zimmermann T, Kim K, Kim KS, Yoon S, Kaplan E, Gualandro DM, Recuenco LH, Huré G, Tsao TY, Nani M, Lee HS, K
resume: Background A novel artificial intelligence-based electrocardiogram (AI-ECG) model (AiTiA MI v2.00.00) for the early diagnosis of acute myocardial infarction (AMI) was developed using data from Korean patients. Its performance in a European population remains unknown. Methods Patients presenting to the emergency department (ED) with suspected AMI were enrolled in two prospective European cohorts (APACE & APACE-Light; ClinicalTrials.gov number, NCT00470587). The primary outcome was AMI, centrally adjudicated according to the fourth Universal Definition of MI. The AI-ECG model was applied to 12-lead ECGs recorded at ED presentation. Its diagnostic performance for AMI was directly compared to that of the BASEL score, high-sensitivity cardiac troponin T (hs-cTnT), the recalibrated HEART score (all at ED presentation), and integrated physician judgment at 90 min, with the last two only available in APACE. Predefined AI-ECG triage thresholds for early rule-out and rule-in of AMI were also evaluated. Findings Among 12,630 patients with an available digital 12-lead ECG (5047 in APACE and 7583 in APACE-Light), adjudicated AMI was diagnosed in 19% (968/5047) and 18% (1386/7583) of patients, respectively. In patients with hs-cTnT at presentation (n = 5031 and n = 7565), the AI-ECG model showed good diagnostic performance for AMI with an area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.78 (95% CI: 0.77-0.80) and 0.84 (0.83-0.85) and an area under the precision-recall curve (AUPRC) of 0.56 (0.53-0.59) and 0.65 (0.62-0.67). Its discrimination was inferior to hs-cTnT (AUC 0.94 [0.93-0.95] and 0.93 [0.92-0.94]). The AI-ECG model provided some incremental diagnostic value when combined with hs-cTnT (AUC 0.95 [0.94-0.96] and 0.95 [0.94-0.95], p Interpretation AI-ECG showed high, but not very high, diagnostic accuracy for AMI. As a diagnosis of AMI is unlikely to be ruled out on ECG alone, combining AI-ECG with hs-cTnT may improve decision making in the ED, warranting prospective studies. titre: Behavior Change Techniques Associated With Abstinence in a Chat-Based Smoking Cessation Intervention: Secondary Analysis of a Randomized Clinical Trial Using Machine Learning.
auteurs: Li Y, Su X, Cheung YTD, Zhao S, Lam TH, Wang MP, Luk TT.
types: research-article randomized controlled trial pragmatic clinical trial journal article
resume: Background Isolating the candidate intervention components that drive the success of digital behavioral interventions is crucial for understanding intervention mechanisms and optimizing future interventions. Objective This study aimed to identify behavior change techniques (BCTs) delivered in a chat-based smoking cessation intervention and determine their independent associations with biochemically validated abstinence. Methods This study is a secondary analysis of a pragmatic, cluster-randomized clinical trial conducted in Hong Kong. From June 18 to September 30, 2017, 624 adult daily smokers were recruited from 34 community sites and randomized to the intervention group. Participants received 3 months of personalized, real-time chat-based cessation support delivered by a live counselor via a mobile instant messaging app. The analytic sample included 230 participants (n=170, 73.9% male; mean age 43.0, SD 13.6 years) who engaged with the chat support. All chat dialogues during the real-time support were retrieved and systematically coded using an established BCT taxonomy for smoking cessation (BCTTsm). Four machine learning methods, least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression, Extreme Gradient Boosting, the Boruta algorithm, and recursive feature elimination, were used to identify the BCTs that are most predictive of biochemically validated tobacco abstinence outcomes at 3 and 6 months. A prespecified supermajority rule retained only BCTs selected by at least 3 of the 4 models for subsequent analysis. The stability of the selected BCTs was assessed using 500 bootstrap resamples for each model. Poisson regression with robust variance was subsequently used to examine the independent associations between the selected BCTs and abstinence outcomes. Covariates included sex, age, educational level, nicotine dependence, intention to quit in 30 days, and quit attempts at baseline. Results Systematic coding identified 35 distinct BCTs from the BCTTsm as having been delivered. Three BCTs were consistently selected by machine learning as the most predictive of both 3- and 6-month abstinence, with moderate to high stability (ranging from 61% to 100%): "provide rewards contingent on successfully stopping smoking" (BM4), "provide information on withdrawal symptoms" (RC6), and "provide information on consequences of smoking and smoking cessation" (BM1). In multivariable analyses, 6-month abstinence was significantly associated with BM4 (risk ratio [RR] 7.9, 95% CI 4.2-14.6), RC6 (RR 3.3, 95% CI 1.6-6.5), and BM1 (RR 2.7, 95% CI 1.4-5.5), with consistent results for 3-month abstinence. Conclusions Three BCTs, contingent rewards (BM4), information on withdrawal symptoms (RC6), and information on consequences (BM1), were identified as candidate intervention components associated with success in a chat-based smoking cessation intervention. This study is the first to apply machine learning for BCT identification, moving beyond simple frequency counts to data-driven feature selection. These findings provide empirical evidence for the candidate components of effective digital behavioral intervention that may warrant further testing and offer guidance for future intervention optimization.

titre: Image-Based AI for the Diagnosis of Retinopathy of Prematurity: Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
auteurs: Bai H, Zhou Y, Bai Y, Wang Y, Yang Y.
types: meta-analysis systematic review review journal article
resume: Background Retinopathy of prematurity (ROP) is one of the major causes of preventable blindness in premature infants. Early screening, accurate diagnosis, and severity classification are crucial for reducing irreversible visual impairment. Recently, image-based AI models have been widely applied to ROP screening, diagnosis, and severity classification. However, the model architecture, data source, validation method, and diagnostic task vary across studies. Consequently, the overall diagnostic efficiency and clinical utility of deep learning (DL) remain to be systematically assessed. Objective This study aims to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of image-based AI for ROP by disease type, validation method, model type, and use of transfer learning (TL). Methods We performed a systematic search across Web of Science, Embase, IEEE Xplore, PubMed, and Cochrane Library as of October 12, 2026, to identify studies investigating image-based AI for ROP detection or clinical subtype classification. The risk of bias (RoB) of included studies was assessed using the Quality Assessment of Diagnostic Accuracy Studies 2 (QUADAS-2) tool. Sensitivity and specificity were pooled using bivariate mixed-effects models, with analyses stratified by diagnostic task and validation method. Results Sixty-two studies contributed 185 contingency tables. For normal vs ROP, pooled sensitivity was 0.94 (95% CI 0.92-0.96) and specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.94-0.97). For normal vs treatment-requiring ROP (TR-ROP), sensitivity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.91-0.99) and specificity was 0.74 (95% CI 0.66-0.80). For mild vs severe ROP, specificity was 0.78 (95% CI 0.59-0.90). In external validation, pooled sensitivity and specificity were 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-0.97) and 0.83 (95% CI 0.72-0.90), respectively, while the corresponding estimates were 0.95 (95% CI 0.93-0.96) and 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) in internal validation. For DL and conventional machine learning (ML) models, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.96 (95% CI 0.90-0.98), respectively, while specificity was 0.96 (95% CI 0.95-0.97) and 0.91 (95% CI 0.84-0.94), respectively. With and without TL, pooled sensitivity was 0.95 (95% CI 0.94-0.96) and 0.95 (95% CI 0.92-0.97), respectively, while specificity was 0.97 (95% CI 0.96-0.98) and 0.92 (95% CI 0.86-0.95), respectively. Conclusions Image-based AI may have high sensitivity for ROP assessment, but its specificity is lower for identifying TR-ROP and in the external-validation subgroup. Given the predominance of retrospective studies, heterogeneity, and limited external validation, current evidence supports AI as an adjunct to screening and referral, with clinicians retaining responsibility for diagnostic and treatment decisions. Prospective, multicenter external validation is needed. Trial registration PROSPERO CRD420261418502; https://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/view/CRD420261418502.

titre: Aortic Valve Stenosis Screening Using Deep Learning on Noninvasive Arterial Pressure Waveforms.
auteurs: Kassab J, Harb SC, Arafati A, Gonzalez Reyes MA, Vlaar APJ, Veelo DP, Kho E, Schenk J, Ramchand J, Collier P, Miyasaka R, Grimm R, Griffin BP, Kapadia SR.
resume: Aortic stenosis (AS) presents a significant health burden. Early identification of significant AS, defined as at least moderate AS, may facilitate timely confirmatory testing, referral, and management. This study sought to develop and externally validate a deep learning model applied to arterial pressure waveforms obtained from a noninvasive finger-cuff system to screen for significant AS, using transthoracic echocardiography as the reference standard. This prospective international multicenter cohort study was conducted from December 2020 through July 2025. Participants underwent concurrent transthoracic echocardiography and noninvasive arterial pressure waveform acquisition. A 1-dimensional convolutional neural network was developed using the Cleveland Clinic development cohort and evaluated in a temporally distinct, multicenter validation cohort including sites in the United States, Spain, and the Netherlands. Significant AS was present in 307 of 3,634 (8.4%) patients in the development cohort and 241 of 1,336 (18.0%) in the validation cohort. In the validation cohort, the model demonstrated an area under the curve of 0.893 (95% CI: 0.876-0.910), with a sensitivity of 92.5% (223/241; 95% CI: 88.5%-95.2%), negative predictive value of 97.5% (706/724; 95% CI: 96.1%-98.4%), specificity of 64.5% (706/1,095; 95% CI: 61.6%-67.3%), and positive predictive value of 36.4% (223/612; 95% CI: 32.7%-40.3%). For severe AS, the area under the curve was 0.906 (95% CI: 0.890-0.922), with a sensitivity of 94.3% (183/194; 95% CI: 90.1%-96.8%), negative predictive value of 98.5% (706/717; 95% CI: 97.3%-99.1%), specificity of 64.5% (706/1,095; 95% CI: 61.6%-67.3%), and positive predictive value of 32% (183/572; 95% CI: 28.3%-35.9%). Deep learning applied to arterial pressure waveforms obtained from a finger-cuff system serves as a promising screening test for significant AS.

titre: A Machine Learning Model for Predicting 28-Day Mortality in Critically Ill Ischemic Stroke Patients With Systemic Inflammatory Response Syndrome: A Retrospective Cohort Study Based on MIMIC-IV and eICU Databases.
auteurs: Liu H, Fan C, Zou J.
resume: Introduction Systemic inflammatory response syndrome (SIRS) commonly complicates ischemic stroke (IS) in critically ill patients and is associated with increased mortality. We aimed to develop and externally validate an interpretable model for predicting 28-day mortality in this population. Methods We used the Medical Information Mart for Intensive Care IV (MIMIC-IV) database for model development and internal validation and the eICU database for external validation. Critically ill IS patients with SIRS during the first ICU day were included. The model predicted mortality occurring between the 24-hour landmark and day 28 after ICU admission. MIMIC-IV patients were randomly divided into training and testing sets at a 7:3 ratio. Least absolute shrinkage and selection operator regression selected predictors for six algorithms. The model with the highest area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) in the testing set was externally validated and compared with the Oxford Acute Severity of Illness Score (OASIS) alone. Performance was assessed using discrimination, calibration, and decision curve analysis. Results The study included 2,438 patients: 1,620 from MIMIC-IV and 818 from eICU. Nine predictors were selected: age, white blood cell count, red blood cell distribution width, blood urea nitrogen, anion gap, Charlson Comorbidity Index, SIRS score, OASIS, and mechanical ventilation. Among the six models evaluated in the testing set, logistic regression (LR) achieved the highest AUC (0.846) and was therefore selected for external validation. In the external validation cohort, the LR model achieved a higher AUC than OASIS alone (0.794 vs. 0.758), and showed reasonable calibration and potential clinical utility. Conclusion We developed and externally validated an interpretable ML-based model for predicting 28-day mortality in critically ill IS patients with SIRS. The LR model showed good discrimination and reasonable calibration in external validation. Prospective multicenter validation and clinical-impact assessment are required before implementation.
